title: Cloud Computing Fundamentals
subtitle: Understand how the cloud works, from service models and regions to compute, storage, networking, access and cost, with AWS, Azure and Google Cloud side by side and labs that need no account.
outcomes: Explain what makes a service cloud computing, and choose between IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and serverless
Describe regions and availability zones, and design for availability across zones
Compare the main compute, storage, database and networking services of AWS, Azure and Google Cloud
Apply the shared responsibility model and least-privilege access to a cloud design
Estimate cloud costs in usage terms and control them with budgets, alerts and tags
prerequisites: No cloud experience needed. Comfort with a terminal (Linux Command Line Essentials) and reading short Python programs (Python Programming with PyCharm) helps. Install Python 3.10 or later, and Node.js or Docker for one lab. No cloud account or payment card is needed. Containerisation and Orchestration with Docker and Kubernetes and Infrastructure as Code with Terraform make good next steps.
description:
Cloud computing runs most of the software people use every day, yet its basics are often buried under product names. This course explains the ideas that stay the same whichever provider you use, and names the services of AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud side by side so you can find your way in any of them. You'll learn what makes something a cloud service, the difference between IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and serverless, who is responsible for what, how regions and availability zones keep services running, and how compute, storage, databases, networks and identity fit together.

Every lab runs on your own computer, with no cloud account and no charges: you'll create and clean up storage through API calls on an emulator, run a serverless function locally, share a private file with a time-limited link on the Azure Storage emulator, plan a network and test a least-privilege policy, and analyse a month of usage against a budget. Optional steps show the free command-line tools for readers with a free-tier account. The capstone has you design a small deployment for all three providers and prove its core flow works locally.

modules.title: What cloud computing is
modules.summary: What makes something a cloud service, the deployment models, the service models from IaaS to SaaS and serverless, and who is responsible for what, with examples from AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud side by side.

lessons.title: Cloud computing defined
objectives: Describe the five essential characteristics of cloud computing
Compare public, private, hybrid and multi-cloud deployments
key_points: The US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) defines cloud computing by five characteristics: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service.

On-demand self-service means you create servers, storage or databases yourself, through a console or an API call, in minutes, without asking anyone; measured service means you pay for what you use, metered by the hour, the second, the gigabyte or the request.

Elasticity means capacity grows and shrinks with demand, often automatically, so you neither buy for the busiest day nor run out on it; resource pooling means many customers share the provider's hardware, kept apart by software.

A public cloud, such as AWS, Microsoft Azure or Google Cloud, is run by a provider for many customers; a private cloud serves one organisation; hybrid cloud connects the two, and multi-cloud uses more than one provider.

Cloud turns up-front capital spending on hardware into an operating cost that follows usage, which helps when demand is uncertain but needs watching, because usage that nobody turns off keeps costing money.

lessons.title: Service models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and serverless
objectives: Distinguish IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and serverless by what you manage
Match common services from AWS, Azure and Google Cloud to each model
key_points: Infrastructure as a service (IaaS) rents virtual machines, disks and networks, and you manage the operating system and everything above it: Amazon EC2, Azure Virtual Machines and Google Compute Engine.

Platform as a service (PaaS) runs your code or data on a managed platform, so you don't patch servers: AWS Elastic Beanstalk, Azure App Service and Google App Engine for applications, and managed databases such as Amazon RDS.
Software as a service (SaaS) is a finished application you use through a browser or an API, such as email, office suites or customer relationship management; you manage your data and who can use it.

Serverless means the provider runs and scales the servers entirely, often down to zero when idle, and bills per request or per unit of work: AWS Lambda, Azure Functions and Google's Cloud Run functions (formerly Cloud Functions) run code in response to events.
Moving from IaaS to SaaS, you control less but manage less; choose the most managed model that still gives you the control you need, because less to manage usually means fewer things to get wrong.

lessons.title: The shared responsibility model
objectives: Explain what the provider and the customer each secure
Show how responsibility shifts between IaaS, PaaS and SaaS
key_points: Security and operations are shared: the provider secures the cloud itself, its data centres, hardware, network and virtualisation, while you secure what you put in it; AWS describes this as security of the cloud versus security in the cloud.
With IaaS you patch and harden the operating system, configure the firewall and manage the software you install; with PaaS the provider patches the platform; with SaaS it runs almost everything.
Some things are always yours, whatever the service model: your data and how it's classified, who has access and with what permissions, and how your accounts and keys are protected.

Many cloud security incidents come from customer-side settings, such as storage left open to the internet or over-generous permissions, so learning your side of the model matters more than worrying about the provider's.

Providers publish their own versions of the model, and Google Cloud also speaks of shared fate, offering secure defaults and blueprints, but the split for each service is in its documentation: read it before you rely on an assumption.

"""Create, use and delete cloud storage with nothing but API calls, against moto's local stand-in for AWS.

Inside the "with mock_aws()" block every AWS call is answered on your computer: no account, no charges.
Run:  python first_calls.py
"""
import os

import boto3
from moto import mock_aws

# Fake credentials, so nothing can ever reach a real account by mistake.
os.environ.update(AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID="testing", AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY="testing", AWS_DEFAULT_REGION="eu-west-1")
REGION = "eu-west-1"
BUCKET = "coop-harvest-reports-demo"


def main():
    with mock_aws():
        ec2 = boto3.client("ec2", region_name=REGION)
        zones = [z["ZoneName"] for z in ec2.describe_availability_zones()["AvailabilityZones"]]
        print(f"Availability zones in {REGION}: {', '.join(zones)}")

        s3 = boto3.client("s3", region_name=REGION)
        s3.create_bucket(Bucket=BUCKET, CreateBucketConfiguration={"LocationConstraint": REGION})
        location = s3.get_bucket_location(Bucket=BUCKET)["LocationConstraint"]
        print(f"Created bucket {BUCKET} in {location}")

        # TODO 1: tag the bucket with team=analytics and cost-centre=cc-104 using put_bucket_tagging,
        # then print the tags that get_bucket_tagging returns.

        for month in ("2025/01", "2025/02", "2025/03"):
            body = f"month,tonnes\n{month},{len(month) * 3}\n".encode()
            s3.put_object(Bucket=BUCKET, Key=f"{month}/summary.csv", Body=body, Metadata={"source": "weighbridge"})
        listing = s3.list_objects_v2(Bucket=BUCKET, Prefix="2025/")
        print(f"Objects under 2025/: {listing['KeyCount']}")
        for obj in listing["Contents"]:
            print(f"  {obj['Key']}  {obj['Size']} bytes")
        head = s3.head_object(Bucket=BUCKET, Key="2025/03/summary.csv")
        print(f"Metadata on 2025/03/summary.csv: {head['Metadata']}")

        # TODO 2: clean up as you would in a real account: delete every object, then the bucket,
        # and print the buckets that are left.


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: get_bucket_tagging returns {"TagSet": [{"Key": ..., "Value": ...}]}: turn it into a dictionary with a comprehension.
list_objects_v2(Bucket=BUCKET)["Contents"] gives the objects to delete with delete_object.
If you see an error about credentials, run the script from a terminal where no real AWS profile is forced on it, or set AWS_PROFILE to nothing.

modules.title: Global infrastructure and compute
modules.summary: Regions, availability zones and edge locations and how to choose between them; the compute options from virtual machines to containers and functions; and designing for availability and elasticity, with a serverless function run locally.

lessons.title: Regions, availability zones and edge locations
objectives: Explain regions, availability zones and edge locations
Choose a region for a workload
key_points: A region is a geographic area with its own set of data centres, such as AWS eu-west-1 in Ireland, Azure West Europe in the Netherlands or Google Cloud europe-west1 in Belgium; most services and their data stay in the region you choose.

An availability zone is one or more data centres in a region with independent power, cooling and networking, close enough for fast links; regions usually have three or more, and spreading across them survives the loss of one.

Naming differs: AWS zones look like eu-west-1a, Google Cloud zones like europe-west1-b, and Azure numbers zones 1, 2 and 3 within a region; on AWS and Azure the same name can map to different physical zones in different accounts.

Edge locations, far more numerous than regions, run content delivery networks and DNS close to users, such as Amazon CloudFront, Azure Front Door and Google Cloud CDN, so content loads quickly worldwide.

Choose a region by where your users are (latency), what the law requires about where data is kept (data residency), which services the region offers, and price, which varies between regions; Azure also pairs many regions for disaster recovery.

lessons.title: Compute options: virtual machines, containers and functions
objectives: Compare virtual machines, containers and functions as ways to run code
Match each to services on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud
key_points: Virtual machines give a whole server to configure, sized by instance or machine type (CPU, memory, sometimes GPUs) and started from an image: the right choice for software that expects a server, or for full control.
Scaling groups run identical VMs from a template and add or remove them with demand: AWS Auto Scaling groups, Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets and Google Cloud managed instance groups.

Containers package an application with its dependencies; managed Kubernetes (Amazon EKS, Azure Kubernetes Service, Google Kubernetes Engine) runs many of them, and serverless containers (AWS Fargate, Azure Container Apps, Google Cloud Run) run them without managing servers.

Functions run a small piece of code per event, such as an HTTP request, a file upload or a message, and scale automatically; they suit short, bursty work but have limits on run time, and the first call after a quiet spell can be slower (a cold start).

Prefer the most managed option that fits: functions or serverless containers for web APIs and event handling, VMs for software that needs a server, and Kubernetes when you run many services and have people to operate it.

lessons.title: Designing for availability and elasticity
objectives: Design an application that survives the failure of a zone
Calculate the availability of components in series and in parallel
key_points: Scale out, adding more instances, rather than up, using a bigger instance: identical instances behind a load balancer, in at least two zones, keep serving when one instance or one zone fails.
Keep instances stateless, with sessions and files in a database, cache or object storage, so any instance can serve any request and new ones can start at any time.
Health checks let a load balancer stop sending traffic to a failed instance, and autoscaling replaces it or adds capacity when a metric, such as CPU use or queue length, crosses a threshold.

Components that all must work are in series, and their availabilities multiply, so the whole is less available than its weakest part; redundant copies are in parallel, and fail only if every copy fails.

A service level agreement (SLA) is the availability a provider commits to, usually with service credits if it's missed; it often requires a multi-zone set-up, so check its conditions before designing to it.

files.content:
"""Availability arithmetic for a simple design. The percentages are assumptions for the exercise,
not any provider's figures: use the ones in your provider's service level agreements.

Run:  python availability.py
"""
MINUTES_PER_30_DAYS = 30 * 24 * 60


def in_series(*parts):
    """Every part must be up: multiply the availabilities."""
    total = 1.0
    for a in parts:
        total *= a
    return total


def in_parallel(*parts):
    """At least one part must be up: 1 minus the chance that all are down (assuming independent failures)."""
    all_down = 1.0
    for a in parts:
        all_down *= 1 - a
    return 1 - all_down


def show(name, a):
    print(f"{name:<44} {a * 100:.4f}%  about {(1 - a) * MINUTES_PER_30_DAYS:.1f} minutes down per 30 days")


def main():
    vm, db, lb = 0.995, 0.999, 0.9999
    show("one VM", vm)
    show("two VMs in different zones", in_parallel(vm, vm))
    show("load balancer + one VM + database", in_series(lb, vm, db))
    show("load balancer + two VMs + database", in_series(lb, in_parallel(vm, vm), db))
    # TODO: add a line for a load balancer, two VMs and a database with a standby in a second zone,
    # where the database pair is in_parallel(db, db).


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: Restart functions-framework after each change to main.py, or add --debug to reload automatically.
Returning a tuple (body, 400) sets the HTTP status code.
in_parallel assumes the copies fail independently, which is why they belong in different zones.

modules.title: Storage and databases
modules.summary: Object, block and file storage; storage classes, lifecycle rules, redundancy and other ways to protect data; and managed relational, NoSQL and analytics databases, with object storage practised on Azurite, the Azure Storage emulator.

lessons.title: Object, block and file storage
objectives: Distinguish object, block and file storage
Choose the right kind for a workload
key_points: Object storage keeps files as objects (data, metadata and a key) in buckets or containers, reached over HTTP, with practically unlimited capacity: Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage and Google Cloud Storage.
Object keys look like paths, such as 2025/03/plot-02.jpg, but the namespace is flat: listing by a prefix gives the effect of folders, and objects are replaced whole rather than edited in place.
Block storage gives a virtual machine a disk that the operating system formats, suited to databases and boot volumes: Amazon EBS, Azure Managed Disks and Google Persistent Disk.
File storage shares a file system between many machines over protocols such as NFS or SMB: Amazon EFS, Azure Files and Google Filestore.
Use object storage for files, backups, data lakes and static websites, block storage for one server's disks, and file storage where several servers need the same folders.

lessons.title: Storage classes, lifecycle and protecting data
objectives: Use storage classes and lifecycle rules to match cost to access
Protect stored data with redundancy, versioning, encryption and limited sharing
key_points: Storage classes trade storage price against access cost and speed: S3 Standard, Standard-IA and the Glacier classes; Azure's Hot, Cool, Cold and Archive tiers; and Google's Standard, Nearline, Coldline and Archive classes.
Colder classes cost less to store but more to read, and often charge a minimum storage duration, so they suit data read rarely; lifecycle rules move or delete objects automatically as they age.

Redundancy copies data within a zone, across zones or to another region; Azure names its options LRS, ZRS, GRS and GZRS, and versioning keeps earlier versions of objects so a mistaken overwrite or delete can be undone.
Object storage is encrypted at rest by default on all three providers, with keys they manage or, if you need control, keys you manage in a key service; encryption doesn't replace access control.
Keep buckets and containers private and share single objects with a time-limited signed link: an S3 presigned URL, an Azure shared access signature (SAS) or a Cloud Storage signed URL.

lessons.title: Managed databases
objectives: Compare relational, NoSQL and analytical database services
Explain what a managed database looks after for you
key_points: Managed relational databases run engines such as PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server for you: Amazon RDS and Aurora, Azure SQL Database and Azure Database for PostgreSQL and MySQL, and Google Cloud SQL, AlloyDB and Spanner.

Managed means the provider installs, patches, backs up and fails over the database server, while you still design the schema, tune queries, choose who can connect and decide how long backups are kept.
High availability puts a standby copy in another zone that takes over automatically; read replicas spread read traffic; point-in-time restore recovers the database to a moment before a mistake.
NoSQL services suit very large scale, flexible records or key-based access: Amazon DynamoDB, Azure Cosmos DB, and Google's Firestore and Bigtable.
Data warehouses analyse large volumes with SQL, storing data by column: Amazon Redshift, Google BigQuery and Microsoft Fabric, as the Data Warehousing and Dimensional Modelling course explains.

"""Object storage on Azurite, the Azure Storage emulator: a private container, blobs with metadata,
listing by prefix, and a time-limited shared access signature (SAS) for one blob.

Start Azurite first (see the lab steps), then run:  python blob_lab.py
"""
import urllib.error
import urllib.request
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

from azure.storage.blob import BlobSasPermissions, BlobServiceClient, ContentSettings, generate_blob_sas

# Azurite's development account. Its name and key are published in Azure's documentation for local
# development only; never use them, or any key written in code, for a real account.
ACCOUNT = "devstoreaccount1"
KEY = "Eby8vdM02xNOcqFlqUwJPLlmEtlCDXJ1OUzFT50uSRZ6IFsuFq2UVErCz4I6tq/K1SZFPTOtr/KBHBeksoGMGw=="
CONTAINER = "field-photos"


def main():
    service = BlobServiceClient.from_connection_string("UseDevelopmentStorage=true")
    container = service.create_container(CONTAINER)          # private: no anonymous access
    print(f"Created container {CONTAINER} at {container.url}")

    for plot in ("plot-01", "plot-02", "plot-03"):
        container.upload_blob(f"2025/03/{plot}.jpg", data=b"\xff\xd8 not really a photo " + plot.encode(),
                              content_settings=ContentSettings(content_type="image/jpeg"),
                              metadata={"farm": "pisac", "crop": "potato"})
    container.upload_blob("2025/04/plot-01.jpg", data=b"\xff\xd8 april")
    march = [b.name for b in container.list_blobs(name_starts_with="2025/03/")]
    print(f"Blobs from March: {march}")
    props = container.get_blob_client("2025/03/plot-02.jpg").get_blob_properties()
    print(f"plot-02: {props.size} bytes, {props.content_settings.content_type}, metadata {props.metadata}")

    blob_url = container.get_blob_client("2025/03/plot-02.jpg").url
    try:
        urllib.request.urlopen(blob_url)
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as err:
        print(f"Anonymous download refused: HTTP {err.code}")

    # TODO: make a read-only SAS for 2025/03/plot-02.jpg that expires in one hour, with generate_blob_sas
    # (account_name=ACCOUNT, account_key=KEY, container_name, blob_name, permission and expiry), download
    # blob_url + "?" + sas with urllib, and print how many bytes came back.

    service.delete_container(CONTAINER)
    print(f"Deleted container {CONTAINER}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: If the script can't connect, check Azurite is still running and listening on port 10000.
An error saying an API version isn't supported means Azurite was started without --skipApiVersionCheck, or needs updating.
The account key in the file is Azurite's published development key; real keys belong in a secret store, never in code.

modules.title: Networking, identity and access
modules.summary: Virtual networks, subnets and routing; firewalls, load balancers and DNS; and identity and access management with least privilege, compared across AWS, Azure and Google Cloud and practised with a network plan and a policy check.

lessons.title: Virtual networks and subnets
objectives: Plan a virtual network with public and private subnets
Compare how AWS, Azure and Google Cloud scope networks and subnets
key_points: A virtual network is your private, isolated network in the cloud, with an address range written in CIDR notation such as 10.20.0.0/16: an Amazon VPC, an Azure Virtual Network (VNet) or a Google Cloud VPC network.

Subnets divide that range; a public subnet routes to the internet through an internet gateway, while a private subnet has no inbound route from the internet and reaches out, for updates, through a NAT gateway.

Scope differs: an AWS VPC belongs to a region and each subnet to one availability zone; an Azure VNet belongs to a region and its subnets span zones; a Google Cloud VPC network is global and its subnets are regional.
Each provider reserves some addresses in every subnet, five on AWS and Azure and four in a Google Cloud subnet's primary range, so a /24 gives 251 or 252 usable addresses rather than 256.
Plan address ranges before you build: avoid overlapping the ranges of your offices and other networks you might connect, and leave space to add subnets later.

lessons.title: Controlling traffic: firewalls, load balancers and DNS
objectives: Control traffic with stateful firewall rules
Describe load balancers, DNS and private connections
key_points: Stateful firewall rules allow inbound and outbound traffic by protocol, port and source, and automatically allow the replies: AWS security groups, Azure network security groups and Google Cloud VPC firewall rules; AWS network ACLs add a stateless layer per subnet.

Open as little as possible: allow web traffic to the load balancer only, allow the application servers to accept traffic only from the load balancer, and never open administration ports such as SSH to the whole internet.

Load balancers spread traffic over healthy instances: layer 4 balancers handle TCP and UDP, layer 7 balancers understand HTTP; examples are AWS Elastic Load Balancing, Azure Load Balancer and Application Gateway, and Google Cloud Load Balancing.
Managed DNS turns names into addresses and can route users to healthy or nearby endpoints: Amazon Route 53, Azure DNS and Google Cloud DNS.
Private connections link your own sites to the cloud without the public internet: a site-to-site VPN, or dedicated links such as AWS Direct Connect, Azure ExpressRoute and Google Cloud Interconnect.

lessons.title: Identity and access management
objectives: Explain identities, permissions and least privilege in the cloud
Compare how AWS, Azure and Google Cloud grant access
key_points: Identity and access management (IAM) decides who, people or software, can do what to which resources; start from nothing allowed, and grant only what each identity needs, which is least privilege.
AWS attaches JSON policies, statements with an Effect, Actions and Resources, to users, groups and roles; anything not allowed is denied, and an explicit Deny overrides any Allow.

Azure assigns roles, such as Reader or Storage Blob Data Reader, to users, groups or managed identities at a scope (a management group, subscription, resource group or resource), using identities from Microsoft Entra ID.

Google Cloud grants roles to principals, such as users, groups and service accounts, on a resource or on a project, folder or organisation, and grants are inherited downwards; predefined roles are safer than the broad basic roles Owner, Editor and Viewer.
Protect the most powerful accounts, such as the AWS root user, with multi-factor authentication and no everyday use, and prefer roles and short-lived credentials to long-lived access keys in code.
Turn on audit logs, AWS CloudTrail, Azure's activity log and Google Cloud Audit Logs, so you can see who did what and when.

files.content:
"""Plan a virtual network: one public and one private subnet in each of three zones, carved from one block.

Run:  python plan_network.py
"""
import ipaddress

NETWORK = ipaddress.ip_network("10.20.0.0/16")
ZONES = ["a", "b", "c"]
RESERVED = {"AWS": 5, "Azure": 5, "Google Cloud": 4}   # addresses each provider keeps in every subnet


def plan():
    small = list(NETWORK.subnets(new_prefix=24))     # 256 blocks of 256 addresses
    large = list(NETWORK.subnets(new_prefix=20))     # 16 blocks of 4,096 addresses
    subnets = {}
    for i, zone in enumerate(ZONES):
        subnets[f"public-{zone}"] = small[i]          # 10.20.0.0/24, 10.20.1.0/24, 10.20.2.0/24
        # TODO: give each zone a private /20 from large, skipping large[0], which holds the public /24s.
    return subnets


def main():
    subnets = plan()
    for name, net in subnets.items():
        usable = ", ".join(f"{p} {net.num_addresses - n}" for p, n in RESERVED.items())
        print(f"{name:<10} {str(net):<15} {net.num_addresses:>5} addresses; usable: {usable}")
    nets = list(subnets.values())
    overlaps = [(a, b) for i, a in enumerate(nets) for b in nets[i + 1:] if a.overlaps(b)]
    print(f"{len(nets)} subnets, overlaps: {overlaps or 'none'}")
    used = sum(n.num_addresses for n in nets)
    print(f"Addresses allocated: {used} of {NETWORK.num_addresses}, leaving room to grow")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""A simplified model of how AWS evaluates identity-based policies, to test a policy before you use it.

Rules: everything is denied unless a statement allows it; an explicit Deny always wins over an Allow.
Actions and resources may use * wildcards. Real AWS adds conditions, resource policies, permission
boundaries and more; Azure RBAC and Google Cloud IAM grant roles at a scope instead, but least privilege
and default deny work the same way.
Usage:  python access_check.py analyst_policy.json
"""
import json
import sys
from fnmatch import fnmatchcase

REQUESTS = [  # (action, resource, what a least-privilege analyst policy should decide)
    ("s3:ListBucket", "arn:aws:s3:::coop-harvest-reports", "ALLOW"),
    ("s3:GetObject", "arn:aws:s3:::coop-harvest-reports/2025/03/summary.csv", "ALLOW"),
    ("s3:PutObject", "arn:aws:s3:::coop-harvest-reports/2025/03/summary.csv", "DENY"),
    ("s3:DeleteObject", "arn:aws:s3:::coop-harvest-reports/2025/03/summary.csv", "DENY"),
    ("s3:GetObject", "arn:aws:s3:::coop-payroll/2025/03/salaries.csv", "DENY"),
    ("ec2:TerminateInstances", "arn:aws:ec2:eu-west-1:111122223333:instance/i-0abc", "DENY"),
]


def as_list(value):
    return value if isinstance(value, list) else [value]


def decide(policy, action, resource):
    allowed = False
    for st in policy["Statement"]:
        if any(fnmatchcase(action, a) for a in as_list(st["Action"])) and \
                any(fnmatchcase(resource, r) for r in as_list(st["Resource"])):
            if st["Effect"] == "Deny":
                return "DENY (explicit)"
            allowed = True
    return "ALLOW" if allowed else "DENY (no statement allows it)"


def main():
    policy = json.load(open(sys.argv[1], encoding="utf-8"))
    passed = 0
    for action, resource, expected in REQUESTS:
        got = decide(policy, action, resource)
        ok = got.startswith(expected)
        passed += ok
        print(f"{'ok  ' if ok else 'FAIL'} {got:<30} {action} on {resource}")
    print(f"{passed} of {len(REQUESTS)} decisions as intended")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: NETWORK.subnets(new_prefix=20) lists the /20 blocks; the first one, 10.20.0.0/20, contains the public /24s.
ListBucket applies to the bucket itself, GetObject to the objects, which is why they need different resources.
In Azure, look at the Storage Blob Data Reader role; in Google Cloud, the Storage Object Viewer role.

modules.title: Cost, budgets and operating well
modules.summary: How cloud pricing works and what drives a bill, how budgets, alerts and tags keep spending under control, and the well-architected frameworks that bring cost, security and reliability together.

lessons.title: How cloud pricing works
objectives: Identify the main drivers of a cloud bill
Compare on-demand, committed and spot pricing
key_points: Most services are pay as you go, and the main drivers are compute time, storage per gigabyte per month, the number of requests, and data transfer: data coming in is usually free, while data going out to the internet, and often between zones or regions, is charged.

On-demand pricing needs no commitment; committing to a level of usage for one or three years earns a discount: AWS Savings Plans and Reserved Instances, Azure reservations and savings plans, and Google Cloud committed use discounts.

Spot capacity, spare capacity sold at a large discount, can be taken back at short notice: AWS Spot Instances, Azure Spot Virtual Machines and Google Cloud Spot VMs suit work that can be interrupted and restarted.

All three providers offer free tiers, some services free up to monthly limits and trial credits for new accounts for a limited time; the terms change, so read the current free tier page, and set a budget before you start.
Each provider has a pricing calculator for estimating a design before you build it; prices differ by region and change over time, so estimate with current figures, never remembered ones.

lessons.title: Budgets, tags and keeping costs under control
objectives: Set budgets and alerts on actual and forecast spend
Use tags and clean-up to find and cut waste
key_points: Budgets alert you when actual or forecast spend passes thresholds, such as 50%, 80% and 100%: AWS Budgets, budgets in Azure Cost Management and Google Cloud Billing budgets; alerts don't stop spending on their own, though they can trigger automation.

Tags in AWS and Azure, and labels in Google Cloud, are key-value pairs such as team=analytics; applied consistently, they show who spends what, and untagged spending is a sign of resources nobody owns.
Common waste includes idle virtual machines, disks left unattached after their server was deleted, old snapshots, oversized instances and test environments left running at night and at weekends.
Rightsizing matches instance size to measured use, scheduling stops non-production resources out of hours, and lifecycle rules move old data to colder storage.
FinOps is the practice of shared financial accountability for cloud spending; the FinOps Foundation's framework describes it as a cycle of three phases: inform, optimise and operate.

lessons.title: Operating well: the well-architected frameworks
objectives: Describe the pillars of the well-architected frameworks
Use monitoring and infrastructure as code to run cloud workloads well
key_points: The AWS Well-Architected Framework has six pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimisation and sustainability.
The Azure Well-Architected Framework has five: reliability, security, cost optimisation, operational excellence and performance efficiency; Google Cloud publishes a similar framework of its own.

The frameworks ask questions rather than prescribe one answer, and review a design against them regularly, because each pillar trades against the others, such as extra zones for reliability costing more.
Monitoring collects metrics, logs and alerts, in Amazon CloudWatch, Azure Monitor and Google Cloud Monitoring, so you see problems, and spending, before your users or the bill do.

Infrastructure as code describes resources in files kept under version control, so environments can be reviewed, repeated and torn down cleanly, as the Infrastructure as Code with Terraform course shows.

files.content:
"""Write a month-to-date usage export for a small cloud account, 1 to 20 March 2025, to usage.csv.

Costs are in credits, a made-up unit for this course: real prices vary by provider, region and date.
Only random.Random(8).random() is used, so the file is the same on every computer.
Run:  python make_usage.py
"""
import csv
import random
from datetime import date, timedelta

rng = random.Random(8)
RESOURCES = [  # resource, service, team, environment, daily cost, average CPU % (None if not a VM), attached
    ("vm-web-1", "compute", "web", "prod", 4.8, 45, True),
    ("vm-web-2", "compute", "web", "prod", 4.8, 40, True),
    ("vm-batch", "compute", "data", "dev", 9.6, 3, True),
    ("vm-test-7", "compute", "", "", 2.4, 1, True),
    ("db-main", "database", "web", "prod", 6.0, None, True),
    ("disk-old-01", "storage", "", "", 0.9, None, False),
    ("bucket-photos", "storage", "data", "prod", 0.5, None, True),
    ("egress", "network", "web", "prod", 2.0, None, True),
]


def main():
    rows = []
    for n in range(20):
        day = date(2025, 3, 1) + timedelta(days=n)
        for name, service, team, env, cost, cpu, attached in RESOURCES:
            if name == "bucket-photos":
                cost = round(0.5 + 0.015 * n, 3)          # storage grows as photos are added
            if name == "egress":
                cost = round(1.0 + rng.random() * 2, 2)   # data sent out to the internet varies by day
            load = "" if cpu is None else round(cpu + rng.random() * 4 - 2, 1)
            rows.append([day.isoformat(), name, service, team, env, cost, load, attached])
    with open("usage.csv", "w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        w = csv.writer(f)
        w.writerow(["date", "resource", "service", "team", "env", "cost_credits", "cpu_avg_pct", "attached"])
        w.writerows(rows)
    print(f"usage.csv: {len(rows)} rows, 2025-03-01 to 2025-03-20")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Month-to-date cost report: where the credits go, what's untagged or idle, and the budget forecast.

Run:  python cost_report.py
"""
import pandas as pd

BUDGET = 900.0                  # credits for March
TODAY = pd.Timestamp("2025-03-20")
DAYS_IN_MONTH = 31
ALERTS = (0.5, 0.8, 1.0)        # alert when actual spend passes these shares of the budget


def load():
    usage = pd.read_csv("usage.csv", parse_dates=["date"], keep_default_na=False, na_values={"cpu_avg_pct": [""]})
    usage["team"] = usage["team"].replace("", "(untagged)")
    return usage


def breakdown(usage):
    print("By service:", usage.groupby("service")["cost_credits"].sum().round(2).to_dict())
    print("By team:", usage.groupby("team")["cost_credits"].sum().round(2).to_dict())
    untagged = usage.loc[usage["team"] == "(untagged)", "cost_credits"].sum()
    print(f"Untagged: {untagged:.2f} credits ({untagged / usage['cost_credits'].sum():.1%} of spend)")


def waste(usage):
    vms = usage[usage["service"] == "compute"].groupby("resource")["cpu_avg_pct"].mean()
    idle = sorted(vms[vms < 5].index)
    unattached = sorted(usage.loc[~usage["attached"], "resource"].unique())
    print(f"Idle VMs (average CPU under 5%): {idle}")
    print(f"Unattached disks: {unattached}")
    return idle + unattached


def forecast(usage, removed=()):
    """Month-to-date spend, plus the last seven days' average daily cost for each day left in the month."""
    actual = usage["cost_credits"].sum()
    recent = usage[(usage["date"] > TODAY - pd.Timedelta(days=7)) & ~usage["resource"].isin(removed)]
    daily = recent.groupby("date")["cost_credits"].sum().mean()
    days_left = DAYS_IN_MONTH - TODAY.day
    return actual, actual + daily * days_left


def budget_status(actual, projected):
    # TODO: print the actual spend and the forecast as shares of BUDGET, then one line for each threshold in
    # ALERTS that actual spend has passed ("ALERT: actual spend passed 50% of the budget"), and a line if the
    # forecast is over 100% ("ALERT: forecast is over the budget").
    pass


def main():
    usage = load()
    breakdown(usage)
    savings = waste(usage)
    actual, projected = forecast(usage)
    budget_status(actual, projected)
    _, after = forecast(usage, removed=savings)
    print(f"Forecast if the idle and unattached resources are removed today: {after:.2f} credits "
          f"({after / BUDGET:.0%} of the budget)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

hints: actual >= share * BUDGET tells you whether a threshold has been passed.
Actual spend hasn't reached 80%, so only the 50% alert and the forecast alert should appear.

project.title: Design a small cloud deployment, side by side
project.brief: A farming co-operative wants a simple web service where members upload photos of their fields and get back a short report, used across one country with a few hundred members. Design it for the cloud and map every part to AWS, Azure and Google Cloud side by side: the service model and compute option for each component, the region and zones, the network with its subnets and firewall rules, the storage and database choices and how data is protected, the identities and least-privilege permissions, and a cost model with a budget and alerts. Then prove the core flow works on your own computer: a function that accepts an upload request, stores the file in object storage on an emulator and returns a time-limited link to it, all without a cloud account.
deliverables: An architecture description or diagram, with a table mapping each component to an AWS, an Azure and a Google Cloud service
A region and zone plan, with the reasons for the region and how the design survives the loss of one zone
A network plan with address ranges, public and private subnets and the firewall rules between them
An access plan: each person or program that needs access, what it may do, and a least-privilege policy or role for at least two of them
A shared responsibility table for every component
A cost model in usage terms (instance hours, gigabytes stored, requests, data out) with a budget, alert thresholds and the tags you would require
A working local prototype using the Functions Framework with Azurite or moto, with its code and a run's output

rubric.name: Architecture and service choices
rubric.description: Each component uses a sensible service model and compute option, justified, and the mapping across the three providers is accurate.

rubric.name: Availability and regions
rubric.description: The region choice is justified; the design survives a zone failure; single points of failure are identified.

rubric.name: Network and security
rubric.description: Subnets and firewall rules expose as little as possible; permissions follow least privilege; the shared responsibility table is correct.

rubric.name: Data protection
rubric.description: Storage classes, redundancy, backups or versioning, encryption and private sharing are chosen deliberately.

rubric.name: Cost and budgets
rubric.description: The cost drivers are identified in usage terms; the budget, alerts and tags are realistic; ways to cut waste are named.

rubric.name: Working prototype
rubric.description: The local prototype stores the upload and returns a working time-limited link, with clear instructions to run it.
